introduction-the-bug-in-the-brain.core: The brain saves energy with shortcuts (heuristics). They're usually useful, but under pressure they produce predictable errors (biases) that engineers must design processes around.

first_principles.problem: Smart engineers still make systematic mistakes in incidents, estimates and post-mortems, because these shortcuts fire automatically.
truths: The brain uses ~20% of the body's energy and conserves it.
Shortcuts are fast but systematically biased.
Knowing a bias doesn't switch it off.
derivation: Learn the **common biases**.
Build **process guardrails** (checklists, devil's advocates, blameless reviews).
Slow down at **high-stakes moments**.

analogy.title: Optical illusions
analogy.story: Even knowing two lines are equal, they still look different. You need a ruler, not willpower.
analogy.breaks: Illusions are static. Biases vary with stress, fatigue and group dynamics.

example.title: 2 a.m. incident
example.scenario: A tired engineer is sure it's the cache, again.

steps.label: Guardrail
steps.detail: The incident template requires evidence for the leading hypothesis.

example.outcome: process catches what tired brains miss.

check.q: Why isn't knowing about a bias enough?
check.a: Biases operate automatically; you need external checks like data and process to counter them.

normalization-of-deviance.core: When a warning sign repeatedly causes no disaster, people start treating it as normal. Risk silently accumulates until it doesn't (Challenger, noisy alerts).

first_principles.problem: 200 alerts fire daily and nobody looks. A flaky test is retried 'because it always fails'. One day the alert or test was real.
truths: Repeated exposure dulls attention.
Lack of disaster isn't evidence of safety.
Small deviations compound.
derivation: Treat **each deviation as a signal** until explained.
Keep **alerts actionable** (delete or fix noisy ones).
Fix or quarantine **flaky tests** with owners.
Periodically ask: **what have we learned to ignore?**

analogy.title: The chirping smoke alarm
analogy.story: Day one you notice the low-battery chirp; by day thirty you no longer hear it, and a visitor asks what the beeping is.
analogy.breaks: A smoke alarm chirps one way. Systems have hundreds of signals, so curate them actively.

example.title: The always-red dashboard
example.scenario: A disk-latency alert fires every day.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Tune or delete noise so every alert means action.

check.q: Where did the term come from?
check.a: Diane Vaughan's study of the Challenger disaster, where O-ring erosion became accepted as normal.

confirmation-bias.core: Once you have a theory, you notice evidence that fits and dismiss evidence that doesn't. In incidents this sends teams down the wrong path for hours.

first_principles.problem: At 2 a.m. you're sure it's the database. Database graphs look odd (they always do) and you ignore the error spike in the auth service.
truths: Theories filter attention.
Disconfirming evidence feels like noise.
Wrong early theories are costly.
derivation: Write **multiple hypotheses**.
Ask **what would prove me wrong?** and look for it.
Assign a **devil's advocate**.
Time-box each hypothesis.

analogy.title: A detective fixated on one suspect
analogy.story: They interpret every clue as pointing to the butler and overlook the alibi.
analogy.breaks: Detectives have time. Incidents need explicit time-boxes to switch hypotheses.

example.title: It must be the DB
example.scenario: Latency spike; the team chases the database for an hour.

steps.label: Habit
steps.detail: Incident lead asks 'what would rule this out?' every 15 minutes.

check.q: What's a practical counter in incidents?
check.a: Ask what evidence would disprove the current theory and check it first.

the-sunk-cost-fallacy.core: Past investment is gone whatever you decide next. Decide based on future costs and benefits, not on how much you've already spent.

first_principles.problem: "We've spent 8 months on this custom platform, we can't stop now." So the team spends 8 more on a project that should have been cancelled.
truths: Spent money and time can't be recovered.
Only future costs and benefits are affected by the decision.
Admitting a mistake feels like waste.
derivation: Ask: **if we were starting today, would we choose this?**
Compare **remaining cost** vs alternatives.
Set **kill criteria** at project start.
Celebrate good cancellations.

analogy.title: Staying for a bad film
analogy.story: You stay because you paid $15. The $15 is gone either way; the real question is how to spend the next 90 minutes.
analogy.breaks: Films end. Software projects can consume effort indefinitely, so kill criteria matter.

example.title: The in-house deploy tool
example.scenario: 8 months in, a managed tool now does 90% of it.

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: Future cost comparison favours the managed tool.

example.outcome: resources move to work that still matters.

check.q: What question cuts through sunk cost?
check.a: "Knowing what we know now, would we start this project today?"

hindsight-bias.core: After an incident, the path to failure looks obvious. It wasn't at the time. Blaming people for 'missing the obvious' blocks learning.

first_principles.problem: A reviewed, tested config change caused an outage. In the post-mortem everyone says 'clearly that was risky', and the engineer is blamed for something nobody saw beforehand.
truths: Outcome knowledge changes perceived predictability.
Decisions should be judged on information available then.
Blame suppresses honest reporting.
derivation: Reconstruct **what was known at the time**.
Ask **why the action made sense** then.
Focus on **system signals that were missing**.
Run **blameless** post-mortems.

analogy.title: Watching a mystery twice
analogy.story: The second time, every clue seems glaring. The first time, you missed them like everyone else.
analogy.breaks: Films show the same clues each time. In real incidents, many signals weren't visible at all.

example.title: Pool size 20 → 50
example.scenario: A reviewed change caused connection exhaustion on the DB.

steps.label: Learning
steps.detail: Staging didn't model production connection counts.

example.outcome: the system gets a missing safeguard instead of a scapegoat.

check.q: How do you counter hindsight bias in a post-mortem?
check.a: Reconstruct what was known at each moment and ask why the action made sense then.

survivorship-bias.core: Looking only at successes hides what killed the failures. Bullet holes on returning bombers showed where planes could survive hits, not where they needed armour.

first_principles.problem: "Every successful startup uses microservices" ignores the many that died from that complexity. Post-mortems only for big incidents miss near-misses.
truths: Failures often leave no data.
Visible successes aren't a random sample.
Missing data can be the most important.
derivation: Ask: **what data is missing?**
Study **failures and near-misses**, not just successes.
Be wary of **success stories** as evidence.

analogy.title: Abraham Wald's bombers
analogy.story: Planes returned with holes in wings and tail. Wald said armour the engines and cockpit: planes hit there never came back.
analogy.breaks: Bomber data was concrete. Engineering failures are often never documented at all.

example.title: Monitoring only crashed services
example.scenario: A team investigates services that crashed, not the ones that silently degraded.

steps.label: Gap
steps.detail: Silent errors never paged, so never got studied.

check.q: What did Abraham Wald recommend and why?
check.a: Armouring where returning planes had no holes, because planes hit there didn't return.

anchoring-bias-in-estimation.core: The first number mentioned anchors estimates, even when it's arbitrary. Protect estimates by estimating independently before discussing and by using reference data.

first_principles.problem: A product manager says "this should take about two weeks, right?" and the team's estimates cluster around two weeks, though the work is closer to six.
truths: First numbers stick.
Adjustment from anchors is insufficient.
Historical data is less biased than gut feel.
derivation: **Estimate independently** first (planning poker).
Use **reference classes**: how long did similar work take?
Avoid stating numbers before estimating.
Estimate in **ranges** with confidence.

analogy.title: Haggling at a market
analogy.story: The seller's first price shapes the whole negotiation, even if it was invented.
analogy.breaks: Market prices can be checked. Software estimates rarely have direct comparables, so record past actuals.

example.title: "Two weeks, right?"

steps.label: Technique
steps.detail: Planning poker before any number is said.

example.outcome: estimates reflect the work, not the first number spoken.

check.q: How does planning poker reduce anchoring?
check.a: Everyone reveals estimates simultaneously, so nobody is influenced by an earlier number.
